messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 68
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: South Asian
- Relationship Status: Divorced
- Occupation: Non-profit Worker
- Trauma Type: Rape
- Pcl5: 76

Mr. Arun Mehta is a sixty-eight-year-old man who presents as soft-spoken and meticulously dressed, his gray kurta pressed and his posture rigid. He has been a program coordinator for a South Asian community non-profit for the past twelve years, a role he took after retiring from a career in accounting. He sits on the edge of the chair, hands clasped in his lap, and speaks in a low, careful voice.

Arun tells me about the night of November 3rd, 2017. He was sixty-one. He had been divorced for four years, living alone in a one-bedroom apartment. A younger man from the temple, a man he had considered a friend, had come over to help him with some paperwork for a charity drive. They had shared a meal, a glass of whiskey. Arun trusted him. He was a respected man in the community, a father. After the meal, the man did not leave. He became aggressive, pinned Arun down on his own sofa, and raped him.

Arun’s voice does not waver as he recounts this. He describes the physical pain, the feeling of his ribs pressing against the cushions, the smell of the man’s cologne—sandalwood and something synthetic. He did not scream. He did not fight back. He says, “I froze. I thought, if I just let it happen, it will be over faster.” The man left afterward, adjusting his shirt, and said, “I hope this doesn’t affect our work.”

Arun did not call the police. He did not tell his daughter, who lives in another state. He did not tell his colleagues. He showered, scrubbing his skin until it was raw. He went to work the next day. He says, “I am a man. Men do not get raped. And if they do, it is their fault. That’s what I thought.”

In the months that followed, Arun’s life contracted. He began to avoid the temple, claiming a new back pain. He stopped attending community dinners, where he might see the man. He stopped taking public transportation, because the press of bodies against him on the bus made his stomach clench. He began to sleep on the floor of his living room, because his bedroom, the site of the assault, felt contaminated. He would lie on a thin mat, staring at the ceiling fan, listening for footsteps.

At work, Arun became withdrawn. He used to be the heart of the office, the one who brought samosas for Diwali and remembered everyone’s birthdays. Now, he keeps his office door closed. He flinches when a colleague touches his shoulder. A few months ago, a young volunteer, a man in his thirties, leaned over his desk to point at a spreadsheet. Arun’s vision went white. He felt the sandalwood cologne, the weight on his chest. He excused himself to the bathroom and vomited.

His daughter calls every Sunday. He tells her he is fine. He tells her he has been busy with the winter coat drive. But he cannot remember the last time he felt present for a conversation. He is constantly scanning the room, cataloging exits. He has lost twenty pounds. He drinks a glass of whiskey every night, not to forget, but to create a barrier of numbness between himself and the world.

The most difficult thing for Arun is the shame. He says, “I was a man. I was older. I should have been able to stop him.” He replays the moment he froze, over and over, and each time, he hates himself a little more. He feels he has been unmade. He is no longer the respected elder, the community pillar. He is a secret, a lie. He lives in a state of constant hypervigilance, his body braced for a threat that never comes, his mind trapped in a room with sandalwood and whiskey and a man he once called a friend.
